guides.title: Literary Theory & the Schools of Criticism
guides.summary: A survey of how literature has been read and interpreted, from classical poetics through formalism, structuralism, and deconstruction to psychoanalytic, Marxist, feminist, postcolonial, and ecological criticism, with the questions each school asks of a text.

sections.heading: What Literary Theory Is and What It Does
sections.body: Literary theory is the systematic reflection on what literature is, how it means, and how it should be read. It stands one step back from ordinary reading and even from ordinary criticism: where a critic interprets a particular poem or novel, the theorist asks what interpretation itself involves, what makes a text literary, where meaning resides, and what a reader is doing when she reads. These questions sound abstract, but they have direct consequences, because how you answer them determines what you notice in a book and what you take a reading to be for. A reader who believes meaning lies in the author's intention will read to recover what the writer meant; one who believes meaning is produced by the reader will attend to her own response; one who believes texts are shaped by class conflict, or by the unconscious, or by structures of language beyond anyone's control, will look for those forces at work. Theory thus supplies the assumptions, often unexamined, behind every act of interpretation, and studying it makes those assumptions visible and open to argument. It is useful to distinguish several recurring questions that organize the whole field. The first concerns the source of meaning: does a text mean what its author intended, what its words say independent of any author, what a reader makes of it, or what the historical and social conditions of its making determined? The second concerns the object of study: is the proper focus the individual work as a self-contained artifact, the system of conventions that makes it possible, the psychology of its creator or reader, or the social and material world it reflects and shapes? The third concerns the purpose of criticism: is it to appreciate beauty, to evaluate quality, to recover historical meaning, to expose hidden ideologies, or to change how we see the world? Different schools of criticism are, in large part, different answers to these questions, each illuminating some aspect of literature while neglecting others. It is a mistake to think of them as a simple progression in which later theories refute earlier ones; rather, they are competing and sometimes complementary lenses, and a sophisticated reader learns to use several. Literary theory drew much of its modern energy from neighboring disciplines, linguistics, psychoanalysis, Marxism, anthropology, philosophy, and its history in the twentieth century is partly the story of literature departments absorbing and adapting ideas from these fields, sometimes to the point of controversy about whether theory had displaced literature itself. This guide surveys the major schools in roughly the order they arose, showing what each contributed, what it left out, and how the whole conversation bears on the practical act of reading a text with understanding. The aim is not to convert the reader to any single theory but to equip her to see how meaning is made and contested.

sections.heading: Classical and Pre-Modern Criticism: Mimesis to Rhetoric
sections.body: Reflection on literature is as old as literature itself, and the categories the ancient world devised still underlie modern debate. In Greece the central idea was mimesis, imitation or representation: literature was understood as an imitation of human life and action. Plato, in the Republic, treated this suspiciously. If the world of appearances is already a copy of the eternal Forms, then art, imitating appearances, is a copy of a copy, twice removed from reality, and Plato worried that poetry stirs the emotions and spreads falsehoods about the gods, leading him to banish most poets from his ideal city. His pupil Aristotle answered this indictment in the Poetics, the founding work of Western literary theory, written in the fourth century BCE. Aristotle defended imitation as natural and instructive, and he analyzed tragedy with an anatomist's precision, identifying its parts, plot, character, thought, diction, melody, and spectacle, and ranking plot as the soul of tragedy. He argued that a well-constructed tragedy arouses pity and fear and achieves catharsis, a purging or clarification of these emotions, and he formulated influential concepts still in use: the tragic hero of high standing brought down not by vice but by an error or flaw, the reversal of fortune, the moment of recognition, and the unity of a plot whose events follow one another by necessity or probability. Where Plato saw danger, Aristotle saw form and function, and his empirical, formal approach set a lasting precedent. The Roman inheritance shifted the emphasis toward rhetoric and craft. Horace, in his verse epistle known as the Art of Poetry, offered practical counsel and the enduring formula that poetry should both delight and instruct, giving pleasure while teaching, and he prized decorum, the fitting of style to subject. The treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus, explored how great writing transports and overwhelms the reader through elevation of thought and intensity of language, introducing an aesthetics of grandeur beyond mere correctness. Through late antiquity and the Middle Ages, literary reflection was largely bound up with rhetoric, grammar, and the interpretation of sacred scripture, where the practice of reading texts on multiple levels, literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical, refined techniques of interpretation that would outlast their theological origin. The Renaissance revived classical poetics, and defenders of poetry such as Philip Sidney, in his Apology for Poetry, answered Puritan attacks by arguing that the poet, unbound by mere fact, can deliver a golden world more instructive than nature's brazen one, teaching virtue more movingly than the philosopher or historian. This long tradition established the questions and vocabulary, imitation, form, genre, emotional effect, the union of pleasure and instruction, decorum, the sublime, that later criticism would inherit, contest, and transform, and it treated literature as a serious art with rules, purposes, and power over the soul.

sections.heading: Romantic and Nineteenth-Century Criticism
sections.body: The late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries brought a profound reorientation in how literature was conceived, a shift the critic M. H. Abrams described as the move from the mirror to the lamp. Where classical and neoclassical theory had treated the poem as a mirror held up to nature, an imitation of the external world governed by rules of craft, the Romantics treated it as a lamp, a projection of the poet's inner life, feeling, and imagination. The emphasis moved from the object represented to the creating subject. William Wordsworth, in the preface to Lyrical Ballads in 1800, a manifesto of English Romanticism, defined poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity, and he rejected the artificial poetic diction of his predecessors in favor of the real language of ordinary people. Samuel Taylor Coleridge supplied the movement's deepest theory, distinguishing the imagination, a living, creative, unifying power that fuses disparate elements into organic wholes, from the mere fancy, which only reassembles fixed materials; he described the willing suspension of disbelief that poetic faith requires and conceived the literary work as an organic form growing from within like a living thing, rather than a mechanical arrangement of parts. This organic conception, the poem as a self-developing unity in which every element is necessary to the whole, would prove enormously influential. Percy Shelley, in his Defence of Poetry, made grand claims for the moral and political power of imagination, arguing that poets, by enlarging our sympathies, are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. The Romantic elevation of genius, originality, imagination, and feeling reshaped the very idea of the author, from a skilled craftsman working within conventions to an inspired individual expressing a unique vision. Later in the century, criticism took several directions. Matthew Arnold, an influential Victorian critic, gave criticism a lofty cultural mission: he defined it as a disinterested endeavor to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world, and he looked to literature, in an age of waning religious faith, to sustain culture and moral seriousness, judging poetry by touchstones of the highest quality. A contrary current, the aestheticism of Walter Pater and the art for art's sake movement, rejected such moralism, insisting that art exists for its own sake and that the proper response to a work is intense, discriminating appreciation of its beauty rather than any moral or social lesson. Meanwhile the rise of realism in fiction prompted its own reflection on how novels represent society and character truthfully. Nineteenth-century criticism thus bequeathed to the modern era a rich but unstable legacy: the exaltation of imagination and the author's inner life, the ideal of the organic unity of the work, the claim that literature carries moral and cultural authority, and the opposing claim that it answers only to beauty, tensions that the theoretical revolutions of the twentieth century would confront directly.

sections.heading: Russian Formalism and the Question of Literariness
sections.body: Modern literary theory in the strict sense begins in the second decade of the twentieth century with a group of Russian scholars who sought to make the study of literature a genuine science with its own object. The Russian Formalists, working in Moscow and in the group known as the Petersburg society for the study of poetic language from around 1915, rejected the reigning approaches that treated literature as a window onto the author's biography, the nation's spirit, or social conditions. They asked instead what makes a verbal work literary at all, and they named their object literariness, the quality that distinguishes literary language from ordinary language. Their answer centered on form and technique rather than content or reference. Ordinary language, they argued, is practical and transparent; we look through it to its message and cease to notice the words themselves. Literary language, by contrast, is self-conscious, foregrounding its own devices, its sounds, rhythms, patterns, and structures, so that the medium becomes palpable. Viktor Shklovsky formulated the movement's most famous concept, ostranenie, usually translated as defamiliarization or estrangement: the function of art, he argued, is to make the familiar strange, to slow down and complicate perception so that we experience things freshly rather than recognizing them automatically. Habit deadens perception, and the techniques of art, by roughening form and delaying understanding, restore the sensation of life. On this view the content of a work, the story it tells, matters less than the devices by which it is told, and Shklovsky provocatively analyzed how a novel's digressions and delays are not obstacles to the story but the very substance of its art. The Formalists distinguished, in narrative, between the fabula, the raw chronological sequence of events, and the sjuzhet, the arrangement in which those events are actually presented in the text, a distinction fundamental to the later study of narrative; a plot's artistry lies largely in how it reorders, withholds, and reveals. In the study of verse, they analyzed sound patterning, meter, and the interplay of rhythm and syntax as the machinery of poetic effect. Roman Jakobson, who bridged Russian Formalism and later structuralism, sought to define the poetic function of language precisely, arguing that it consists in projecting the principle of equivalence from the axis of selection onto the axis of combination, meaning that in poetry, elements that are merely similar, in sound or grammar, are set in sequence, so that likeness in rhyme, meter, and parallelism becomes the organizing principle of the message. The Formalists were suppressed under Soviet ideological pressure by the early 1930s, condemned for ignoring the social content of literature, but their ideas survived through émigrés and through the Prague School, and they laid the groundwork for structuralism, narratology, and the whole modern concern with the specifically literary properties of texts. Their lasting contribution was to insist that criticism attend to how a work is made, treating literature as a craft of language with analyzable techniques rather than a mere vehicle for biography or ideas.

sections.heading: New Criticism and Close Reading
sections.body: In the English-speaking world, the dominant approach to literature from roughly the 1930s through the 1950s was the New Criticism, a movement centered in the United States and Britain that transformed how literature was taught and read. Like the Russian Formalists, whom they resembled without direct influence, the New Critics insisted that the poem itself, its words on the page, is the proper object of study, and they resisted the tendency to reduce a work to its author's biography, its historical background, or its emotional effect on readers. Their positive method was close reading, the patient, detailed analysis of the language of a text, attending to its imagery, ambiguity, irony, paradox, tension, and structure, on the conviction that a poem is a complex verbal artifact whose meaning is embodied in the precise interplay of its words and cannot be paraphrased without loss. Cleanth Brooks called this the heresy of paraphrase, the mistake of thinking a poem's meaning can be restated in other words; the poem means what it is, an organized structure of tensions resolved into unity. The New Critics prized the well-wrought urn, the poem as a self-sufficient whole whose apparent contradictions are held in balance, and they especially admired the metaphysical poets and any verse rich in irony and ambiguity. William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity demonstrated how much interpretive richness careful attention to multiple meanings could yield, while I. A. Richards pioneered practical criticism by showing how unreliably even trained readers judged poems stripped of their authors' names, arguing for disciplined, text-focused reading. The theoretical backbone of the movement was supplied in two influential essays by W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley. The intentional fallacy warns against judging a work by reference to the author's intention, which is neither available nor decisive; what matters is what the words actually achieve, not what the writer meant to do. The affective fallacy warns against confusing the poem with its emotional effects on the reader, which vary and cannot ground objective interpretation. Together these arguments sealed the text off from both author and reader, locating meaning firmly in the verbal object itself. The New Criticism had enormous pedagogical value, for it gave students and teachers a portable technique, close reading, that required no specialized historical knowledge and could be applied to any text, and it professionalized literary study. But its limitations drew increasing criticism. By treating the poem as a timeless, autonomous artifact, it tended to ignore history, politics, and the social conditions of literature; by focusing on short lyric poems suited to close analysis, it was less at home with long novels and their sprawling engagement with society; and its claim of objectivity concealed value judgments about which works were worth studying. Later theory would reopen everything the New Criticism had closed off, the author, the reader, history, ideology, but the discipline of close reading it perfected remains an indispensable skill, and even critics who reject its premises still practice the careful attention to language it taught.

sections.heading: Structuralism and Narratology
sections.body: Structuralism was the most ambitious theoretical movement of the mid-twentieth century, and it applied to literature and culture the model of language developed by Ferdinand de Saussure. Saussure had argued that a language is a system in which signs have meaning not in themselves but through their differences from other signs, and that the proper study is of the underlying system, langue, rather than individual utterances, parole. Structuralists generalized this insight into a method for analyzing any system of signs, holding that the meaning of any cultural element, a word, a gesture, a dish, a fashion, a story, derives from its place within a structure of relations and oppositions. The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss applied the model to myth, arguing that beneath the endless diversity of myths lie a small number of underlying structures built from binary oppositions, such as raw and cooked or nature and culture, which the myth works to mediate; the individual myth is a variation on deep patterns the analyst can uncover. In literary study this program produced narratology, the systematic science of narrative, which seeks the universal grammar underlying all stories. An early inspiration was Vladimir Propp, a Russian scholar who, analyzing a corpus of folktales, found that beneath their varied surfaces lay a fixed sequence of a limited set of functions, actions defined by their role in the plot, such as the hero leaving home, being tested, or defeating a villain, always occurring in the same order though not all present in every tale. Later narratologists such as A. J. Greimas, Tzvetan Todorov, Roland Barthes in his structuralist phase, and above all Gérard Genette built elaborate frameworks for describing how narratives work. Genette distinguished with great precision the levels of narrative: the order in which events are told versus the order in which they happen, allowing analysis of flashback and anticipation; the duration and frequency of narration; the difference between who sees, the focalizer, and who speaks, the narrator; and the various relations between narrator and story. Structuralist poetics, exemplified by Jonathan Culler's account, shifted attention from interpreting individual works to describing the system of conventions, the literary competence, that enables readers to make sense of texts at all, asking not what a poem means but how it comes to be readable as a poem. The appeal of structuralism was its promise of rigor and objectivity, a genuine science of literature grounded in the analysis of systems rather than the impressions of individual critics, and its influence spread across the humanities and social sciences. Its limitations, however, prompted the reaction that followed. In seeking timeless underlying structures, it tended to neglect history, change, and the individual work's particularity; in treating the human subject as merely a position within a system, it seemed to dissolve the author and the reader into anonymous structures; and its confidence that structures could be objectively identified would soon be challenged by thinkers who had begun within structuralism itself and turned against its assumptions.

sections.heading: Post-Structuralism and Deconstruction
sections.body: Post-structuralism emerged in France in the late 1960s from within structuralism, accepting its starting point, that meaning is produced by systems of signs rather than by things or intentions, but radicalizing it to undermine the stability structuralism had sought. If, as Saussure held, signs mean only through their differences from other signs, the post-structuralists argued, then meaning is never fully present in any sign but is endlessly deferred along chains of signification, and the structuralist dream of pinning down fixed underlying structures collapses. The central figure is Jacques Derrida, whose method of reading, deconstruction, he introduced in works published around 1967. Derrida argued that Western thought has been governed by a metaphysics of presence that privileges speech over writing and craves a stable center or ground of meaning, and that it organizes itself through hierarchical binary oppositions, presence over absence, speech over writing, nature over culture, man over woman, in which the first term is treated as primary and the second as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction shows that these hierarchies are unstable: close reading reveals that the privileged term secretly depends on the subordinate one, that the oppositions cannot be maintained, and that texts undermine their own apparent claims. He coined the term différance, playing on the French for both to differ and to defer, to name the way meaning is generated by differences and perpetually postponed, never arriving at a final signified. His often-quoted assertion that there is nothing outside the text is best understood not as a denial of reality but as the claim that we have no access to meaning except through the endless play of signification, with no anchoring point outside language that would halt interpretation. In the United States, deconstruction was taken up by critics associated with Yale, notably Paul de Man, who argued that literary language is fundamentally rhetorical and figurative, so that every text contains contradictions between what it says and what it does, between its grammatical and its rhetorical dimensions, making any final, coherent interpretation impossible; reading, on this view, is the discovery of a text's inevitable undecidability. Post-structuralism was not only Derrida. Roland Barthes, moving beyond his structuralist phase, proclaimed the death of the author, arguing that a text is not a message from an originating author to be decoded but a tissue of quotations drawn from innumerable sources of culture, whose unity lies in its destination, the reader, not its origin; meaning is produced in reading, not deposited by writing. This dethroning of the author and of stable meaning was liberating and disturbing in equal measure. Critics charged that deconstruction, by making every text undecidable and denying any ground for interpretation, led to relativism and interpretive paralysis, and that its intricate wordplay could become an end in itself. Defenders replied that it fosters a rigorous humility about the limits of interpretation and a heightened attention to the workings of language, exposing the hidden assumptions and suppressed contradictions in texts and in the very concepts, truth, presence, origin, that other theories take for granted. Whatever one concludes, post-structuralism permanently unsettled the confident objectivity of both structuralism and the New Criticism.

sections.heading: Psychoanalytic Criticism
sections.body: Psychoanalytic criticism reads literature through the theories of the unconscious mind developed by Sigmund Freud and his successors, on the premise that literary works, like dreams, jokes, and slips of the tongue, express desires and conflicts that are hidden from conscious awareness. Freud held that the mind is divided, that much of mental life is unconscious, and that repressed wishes, especially those arising in early childhood and often sexual in nature, return in disguised form. Because art resembles the disguised fulfillment of a wish, literature offered Freud a natural field, and he himself analyzed works, most famously reading the myth of Oedipus and Shakespeare's Hamlet in terms of the Oedipus complex, the child's forbidden desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent, arguing that Hamlet's paralysis expresses his own repressed guilt. Early psychoanalytic criticism took several forms. One approach treated the literary work as a symptom of its author's psyche, reading the text to uncover the writer's neuroses and repressed conflicts, an approach vulnerable to the objection that it reduces art to biography and treats characters as if they were real patients. A second approach analyzed characters within the work as psychological cases, illuminating their motives through concepts such as repression, projection, and the unconscious. A third, more defensible approach attends to the reader's psychology, asking how literature engages the unconscious desires and fears of its audience, why we take pleasure in tragedy or horror, and how identification and fantasy operate in reading. The most influential reworking of psychoanalysis for literary theory came from the French analyst Jacques Lacan, who reinterpreted Freud through the lens of structural linguistics, declaring that the unconscious is structured like a language. Lacan's account of the mirror stage describes how the infant forms an illusory sense of a unified self by identifying with its image, so that the ego is founded on a misrecognition; and his distinction among three registers, the imaginary, the symbolic, the order of language and law into which we are inducted, and the real, that which resists symbolization, gave critics a rich vocabulary. For Lacan desire is bound up with language and with a fundamental lack that can never be filled, and the subject is decentered, not master in its own house, an idea that converged with post-structuralism's suspicion of the unified self. Later theorists combined psychoanalysis with feminism and film theory; the concept of the gaze, developed in Laura Mulvey's analysis of how cinema positions the spectator and objectifies the female figure, drew on Lacanian ideas to political effect. Psychoanalytic criticism has been sharply contested. Skeptics question the scientific standing of psychoanalysis itself, warn against the circularity of an interpretation that can explain any evidence and its opposite, and object that finding phallic symbols and Oedipal patterns everywhere can become a mechanical exercise that flattens the specificity of works. Yet at its best the approach takes seriously that literature moves us at levels below conscious understanding, that reading can be an encounter with what we do not fully know about desire, loss, and the self, making it a durable, if disputed, resource of criticism.

sections.heading: Marxist and Materialist Criticism
sections.body: Marxist criticism reads literature in relation to the economic and social conditions that produce it, insisting that art is not a timeless expression of universal human nature but a product of history, shaped by the material realities of its age and by the conflicts among social classes. Its foundation is Karl Marx's claim that the economic base of a society, its mode of production and the relations of ownership and labor it entails, conditions the superstructure of law, politics, religion, philosophy, and art, so that the ideas and cultural forms of an era tend to reflect and serve the interests of its dominant class. From this follows the concept of ideology, understood as the ways in which a society's beliefs, including those embodied in literature, present the particular interests of the ruling class as natural, universal, and inevitable, and thereby help reproduce an unjust order. Marxist critics therefore ask what a literary work reveals, often unintentionally, about the class relations and ideological assumptions of its time: whose interests its values serve, what it makes visible and what it silently excludes, how its very form encodes a social vision. The tradition is rich and internally varied. Georg Lukács, a Hungarian critic, championed the realist novel of the nineteenth century for its capacity to represent the totality of social relations and to show individuals as historically situated types, and he criticized modernist fragmentation as a symptom of alienation. Against him, Bertolt Brecht argued for an anti-illusionist art that breaks the spell of realism, using devices of estrangement to make the audience think critically about social conditions rather than lose themselves in the story. The Frankfurt School theorists Theodor Adorno and Walter Benjamin explored the fate of art under capitalism from opposed angles: Adorno defended difficult, autonomous modern art as a refuge of critical negativity against the deadening culture industry of mass entertainment, while Benjamin, more hopefully, examined how mechanical reproduction, in film and photography, might strip art of its aura and open new political possibilities. The French Marxist Louis Althusser reconceived ideology not as false consciousness but as the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real conditions, a system that hails or interpellates individuals as subjects and that operates through institutions, and his ideas shaped a generation of critics, including Pierre Macherey, who argued that a text's significant silences and gaps reveal the ideological contradictions it cannot openly express. The most influential figure in Anglophone Marxist criticism, Fredric Jameson, urged critics always to historicize and analyzed how narrative form itself carries a political unconscious, encoding and managing the social contradictions of its moment. Marxist criticism has been faulted for sometimes reducing complex works to reflections of economic conditions, for subordinating aesthetic value to political judgment, and for the failures of the regimes that invoked Marx, and later Marxists took pains to grant art a relative autonomy rather than treat it as a mere mirror of the base. Yet the tradition permanently enriched criticism by insisting that literature is embedded in history and power, that form and ideology are inseparable, and that reading can expose the social interests hidden within apparently innocent stories.

sections.heading: Feminist, Gender, and Queer Theory
sections.body: Feminist criticism, which emerged as a major force with the women's movement of the late 1960s and 1970s, reads literature with attention to gender, exposing how texts and the traditions that canonize them have represented, marginalized, and been shaped by women, and challenging the assumption that a supposedly universal, neutral perspective is in fact a male one. Its concerns are several. One is critique of the representation of women in works by men, analyzing the stereotypes, the angel and the monster, the virgin and the whore, and the ways literature has encoded patriarchal attitudes; Kate Millett's Sexual Politics offered an early, combative example, reading canonical male authors for their sexual ideology. A second concern is the recovery of women writers unjustly neglected by a male-dominated canon, and the study of a distinct female literary tradition; Elaine Showalter named this project gynocriticism, the study of women as writers, their history, themes, and forms, and Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar, in The Madwoman in the Attic, influentially examined the anxieties and strategies of nineteenth-century women writers working within and against a patriarchal tradition, reading the rebellious madwoman as the author's double. A foundational text behind all this was Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, which argued that women's literary achievement had been constrained by material conditions, the lack of money, education, and independent space, and imagined the thwarted fate of a hypothetical sister of Shakespeare. French feminist theory, drawing on psychoanalysis and post-structuralism, took a different path: Hélène Cixous and Luce Irigaray explored the idea of a specifically feminine writing that might escape the masculine structures of language, while Julia Kristeva analyzed the disruptive, pre-symbolic dimension of language. A crucial development was the distinction between biological sex and socially constructed gender, and the recognition, pressed by Black feminists such as bell hooks and by the concept of intersectionality named by Kimberlé Crenshaw, that gender cannot be analyzed in isolation from race, class, and sexuality, since women's experiences differ profoundly across these axes. From these roots grew gender studies and queer theory, which extended the analysis to sexuality and to the very categories of male and female, gay and straight. Judith Butler's Gender Trouble argued that gender is not the expression of a prior inner essence but is performatively produced, constituted through repeated stylized acts that create the illusion of a natural, stable identity, a claim that destabilized the notion of fixed sexual identity itself. Queer theory, drawing also on Michel Foucault's history of sexuality, which argued that the homosexual as a type of person was a relatively recent historical construction rather than a timeless natural kind, and on Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's analysis of how the hetero-homosexual distinction structures modern culture, reads literature for the instability of sexual categories and for desires and identities that exceed the normative. These interlocking approaches transformed the discipline, reshaping the canon, the questions asked of texts, and the understanding that gender and sexuality are not natural givens but constructed, contested, and inscribed in the language and forms of literature.

sections.heading: Postcolonial Criticism
sections.body: Postcolonial criticism examines literature in relation to the history of European colonialism and its aftermath, analyzing how colonized peoples were represented, how imperial power shaped culture and knowledge, and how writers from formerly colonized societies have contested and rewritten the inherited traditions. Its founding text is Edward Said's Orientalism of 1978, which analyzed the vast body of Western scholarship, literature, and art about the East and argued that Orientalism was not neutral knowledge but a discourse, in Foucault's sense, that produced the Orient as an exotic, irrational, backward Other against which the West defined itself as rational and superior, and that this discourse was bound up with, and helped justify, imperial domination. Said showed that even canonical European literature was implicated in empire, and his method, reading texts for the assumptions and power relations of colonialism, opened a new field. Two other theorists shaped its dominant form. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, translating Derrida and combining deconstruction, Marxism, and feminism, posed in a famous essay the question of whether the subaltern, the most oppressed and voiceless colonized subject, especially the colonized woman, can speak, or whether they are always spoken for and represented by others, warning against the intellectual's presumption to give them voice. Homi Bhabha, drawing on psychoanalysis and post-structuralism, developed concepts that complicate the simple opposition of colonizer and colonized: hybridity, the mixed, in-between cultural identities produced in the colonial encounter; mimicry, the way the colonized are encouraged to imitate the colonizer yet, being almost the same but not quite, produce a menacing, subversive difference; and the ambivalence at the heart of colonial authority. Behind these academic theorists stood earlier anticolonial writers, notably Frantz Fanon, whose analyses of the psychology of colonization, the internalized inferiority it induces and the role of violence in liberation, remain foundational. Postcolonial criticism reexamines the Western canon, producing readings such as those of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, which the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe attacked as dehumanizing Africa, or of Jane Eyre reread through the silenced Creole woman in the attic, a reading dramatized in Jean Rhys's novel Wide Sargasso Sea, which retells the story from her perspective. Equally important, it studies the rich literatures produced across Africa, the Caribbean, South Asia, and other formerly colonized regions, including the fraught question of language, whether a writer should use the colonizer's tongue, as many do to reach a global audience, or write in indigenous languages, a choice the Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o made as an act of decolonization. Related fields, such as the study of diaspora, migration, and globalization, and the critique of how the very category of world literature is constructed, extend the inquiry. Critics have debated whether postcolonial theory, often written in dense academic prose within Western universities, adequately serves the peoples it studies, and whether its focus on discourse and identity neglects material inequality. Yet it decisively broadened literary study beyond the European tradition, insisting that literature and empire are entangled and that the reading of texts is inseparable from the global history of power, resistance, and cultural exchange.

sections.heading: Reader-Response, New Historicism, and Cultural Studies
sections.body: Several influential movements shifted the focus of criticism away from the isolated text toward, respectively, the reader, the historical archive, and the whole field of culture. Reader-response criticism, which gained prominence in the 1970s, challenged the New Critical dogma that meaning resides objectively in the text, arguing instead that a literary work exists only in the act of reading and that readers actively produce meaning rather than passively receiving it. Wolfgang Iser argued that texts are full of gaps and indeterminacies that the reader must fill, so that reading is a dynamic collaboration, while Stanley Fish provocatively contended that even the features we ascribe to a text are produced by the interpretive strategies we bring to it, and that meaning is determined by interpretive communities, the shared assumptions of groups of readers, rather than by the words alone. This approach usefully foregrounded the activity of reading but raised the worry that if readers make meaning freely, any interpretation is as good as any other, a relativism its defenders sought to limit by appeal to shared conventions. New Historicism, associated above all with Stephen Greenblatt and emerging in the 1980s in reaction to the ahistorical formalism of the New Criticism and the textual self-enclosure of deconstruction, returned criticism to history but in a new way. Rather than treating history as a stable background against which literature is set, New Historicists treat literary and non-literary texts as equally part of a single cultural fabric, reading a play alongside a medical treatise, a travel narrative, a legal record, or an account of an exorcism, and tracing the circulation of ideas, anxieties, and forms of power among them. Influenced by Foucault's analysis of power as dispersed and productive, they attend to how literature participates in the negotiation and containment of social energies, neither simply reflecting its age nor standing apart from it. A related British movement, cultural materialism, associated with Raymond Williams and Alan Sinfield, shared the historical turn but placed more emphasis on the political uses of literature in the present and on culture as a site of ongoing struggle. Broader still is cultural studies, which grew from the work of Williams, Richard Hoggart, and Stuart Hall at Birmingham and expanded the object of analysis beyond canonical literature to popular and mass culture, television, advertising, music, subcultures, and everyday practices, on the democratic principle that these are as worthy of serious study as high art and as revealing of how power, identity, and meaning operate in society. Stuart Hall's model of encoding and decoding showed how audiences actively interpret media messages, sometimes against their intended meaning. Cultural studies blurred the boundary between literary criticism and the social sciences and shifted attention toward questions of ideology, identity, and reception across the whole range of cultural production. Together these movements decentered the literary text: reader-response relocated meaning in reception, New Historicism dissolved the boundary between literary and historical documents, and cultural studies expanded the field to all of culture, so that the very definition of the object of study, once assumed to be the canonical literary work, became an open and contested question.

sections.heading: Ecocriticism, Digital Humanities, and the Future of Theory
sections.body: The most recent developments in literary theory reflect new preoccupations of the wider world, above all the environmental crisis and the digital transformation of texts, while the field as a whole has entered a more pluralistic and self-questioning phase. Ecocriticism, which emerged as an organized approach in the 1990s, reads literature in relation to the natural environment, analyzing how texts represent nature, place, and the relationship between humans and the non-human world, and how literary imagination might shape ecological awareness in an age of climate change and mass extinction. It began by studying nature writing and the pastoral tradition and by recovering the environmental dimension of canonical works, but it has grown more theoretically ambitious, drawing on the concept of the Anthropocene, the proposed epoch in which human activity has become a geological force, and asking how literary forms can represent phenomena, like global warming, that unfold on scales of time and space beyond ordinary human perception, what the critic Timothy Morton calls hyperobjects. Related currents, including animal studies, which questions the human-animal boundary, and the broader turn toward the material and the non-human sometimes called new materialism or posthumanism, challenge the anthropocentric assumptions of earlier theory. The digital humanities represent a different frontier, applying computational methods to literary study: the analysis of vast archives of texts by machine, what Franco Moretti called distant reading, in contrast to the close reading of individual works, seeks large-scale patterns across thousands of books, in genre, style, or the circulation of themes, that no individual reader could perceive. These methods provoke debate about whether quantification can capture what matters in literature or whether it merely counts what is countable. The broader condition of theory in the present is one after the era of grand theoretical systems, the decades from the 1960s through the 1980s when structuralism, deconstruction, and their rivals seemed to promise total accounts of how literature works. Some speak of a return to questions of form, of aesthetics, of ethics, and of the reasons literature gives pleasure and matters; the critics Rita Felski and others have questioned the reflex of reading always to unmask and expose, and called for attention to what literature offers, enchantment, knowledge, recognition, as well as to what it conceals. What endures from the century of theory surveyed here is not any single victorious school but a set of permanent gains: the discipline of close attention to language from formalism and New Criticism; the awareness that meaning is made in systems and unsettled by their instabilities from structuralism and post-structuralism; the recognition that literature is entangled with the unconscious, with class, with gender and sexuality, with empire, and with the environment, from the ideological criticisms; and the understanding that reading is an active, situated, and consequential act. The practical lesson for a reader is that no single lens is sufficient, that each school reveals what others hide, and that to read well is to bring a repertoire of questions to a text and to remain aware of the assumptions one is making, so that interpretation becomes a conscious, disciplined, and endlessly renewable art.

guides.title: What Is Literature? An Introduction to Literary Study
guides.summary: A comprehensive introduction to the study of literature: how the field defines its object, the major genres of poetry, narrative, and drama, the tools of close reading and figurative language, literary history and criticism, and the enduring questions of value, meaning, and where interpretation lives.

sections.heading: The Problem of Defining Literature
sections.body:
It seems obvious what literature is, until one tries to define it, at which point the boundaries dissolve. We readily call a Shakespeare play, a novel by Tolstoy, and a poem by Emily Dickinson literature, yet we hesitate over a well-crafted advertisement, a gripping true-crime article, or a beloved genre thriller. The difficulty of drawing the line is not a failure of thought but a genuine feature of the subject, and grappling with it is the proper first step in literary study.

Several definitions have been proposed, each capturing something and none sufficing alone. One approach defines literature by its language: literary writing, on this view, uses language in a special, heightened, self-conscious way, foregrounding rhythm, imagery, ambiguity, and form so that how something is said matters as much as what is said. The Russian Formalists of the early twentieth century called this quality defamiliarization, the power of literary language to make the familiar strange and thus perceptible again. Yet plenty of ordinary speech is figurative, and much prized literature is written plainly, so this criterion is suggestive rather than decisive.

A second approach defines literature by its fictionality, its imaginative rather than factual character. But this excludes essays, histories, and memoirs long counted as literature, and it fails to explain why some fiction is treated as literature and other fiction as mere entertainment. A third approach appeals to enduring value, defining literature as writing judged to possess lasting aesthetic or moral worth, the works a culture preserves, teaches, and rereads. This captures how the word is often used but is circular and unstable: it makes literature whatever we happen to value, and it cannot explain how new works enter, or old ones leave, the category.

The critic Terry Eagleton pressed this problem to a provocative conclusion, arguing that literature has no essence at all, that it is not an objective property of texts but a label a society attaches to writing it esteems, so that the category shifts with time and power. What one age calls literature another ignores; works by many women and colonized peoples were long excluded, then later admitted. On this view literature is a value judgment, and its history is partly a history of taste and authority.

For the student, the useful lesson is not to seek a single airtight definition but to hold these criteria together as overlapping family resemblances. A text is more likely to be treated as literature the more it uses language artfully, invites interpretation rather than yielding a single message, rewards rereading, and is embraced by a community of readers as worth preserving. Literary study begins precisely where the boundary is uncertain, in the questions of what makes writing worth close attention and who gets to decide.

sections.heading: Genre: The Major Kinds of Literary Writing
sections.body:
Faced with the vast field of written art, readers and critics have always sorted it into kinds, or genres, and understanding this system of classification is basic to literary study. A genre is a category defined by shared conventions of form, technique, subject, or effect, and it functions as a set of expectations that both writers and readers bring to a text. When a work announces itself as a tragedy, a sonnet, or a detective story, it activates a framework that guides interpretation, and much of a work's meaning comes from how it fulfills, bends, or breaks those expectations.

At the broadest level, the Western tradition since Aristotle has recognized three great modes. The lyric is the mode of the speaking voice expressing thought and feeling, typically short and associated with poetry. The dramatic is the mode of enacted action, in which characters speak and behave before an audience without a narrator's mediation, the domain of the play. The epic or narrative is the mode of story told by a narrator, encompassing the epic poem and, in modern times, the novel and short story. These modes are not rigid boxes; a novel may contain lyric passages and dramatic dialogue, but the threefold scheme organizes the field.

Within these modes lie the more specific genres familiar from any bookshelf. Poetry subdivides into forms such as the epic, the ode, the elegy, and the sonnet. Prose fiction ranges across the novel and its subgenres, the novella, and the short story. Drama divides classically into tragedy, which traces a serious action to a grave and often catastrophic end, and comedy, which moves through complication to a happy resolution, with many hybrids between. A fourth great category, nonfiction prose, includes the essay, biography, autobiography and memoir, and history when written with literary art.

Genres are historical, not eternal. They arise, flourish, transform, and sometimes fade, in response to changing tastes, technologies, and societies. The novel, now the dominant literary form, scarcely existed before the eighteenth century and rose with print, literacy, and a reading middle class. Genres also blend and multiply: the twentieth century produced the nonfiction novel, magical realism, and countless crossings of high and popular forms.

For the student, genre is a double-edged tool. It provides indispensable orientation, telling us how to read, what kind of coherence to look for, and which conventions are in play, so that we do not fault a fable for being improbable or a lyric for lacking plot. But genre can also mislead if treated as a straitjacket, since the most interesting works often achieve their power precisely by violating the expectations of their kind. The skilled reader uses genre as a starting hypothesis about a text, held firmly enough to guide attention and loosely enough to be surprised.

sections.heading: Poetry: Form, Meter, and Sound
sections.body:
Poetry is the oldest literary art, predating writing itself in oral tradition, and it is distinguished by its intense attention to the sound, rhythm, and shape of language. Where prose runs continuously to the margin, poetry is written in lines, and the line is poetry's fundamental unit: the poet chooses where each line ends, and that choice, the line break, controls pace, emphasis, and meaning in ways prose cannot. To read poetry well is to attend to the line, the sentence, and the tension between them.

Much traditional poetry is organized by meter, a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. In English, the dominant meter is the iamb, a unit of one unstressed followed by one stressed syllable, as in the word before or the phrase the sun. A line of five iambs is iambic pentameter, the meter of Shakespeare's plays and sonnets and of Milton's epic, and its rhythm, heard in a line like shall I compare thee to a summer's day, approximates the natural cadence of English speech while heightening it. Other feet include the trochee, the anapest, and the dactyl, and the interplay between a poem's underlying metrical pattern and the actual rhythm of its words, the moments where a stress falls unexpectedly, is a chief source of poetic effect.

Sound binds poetry as much as rhythm. Rhyme, the matching of end sounds, organizes many traditional forms, but poets deploy a wider palette: alliteration, the repetition of initial consonants, as in the winds of winter; assonance, the repetition of vowel sounds; consonance; and onomatopoeia, words that imitate sounds. These devices are not decoration; they knit words together, slow or quicken the ear, and forge connections of meaning between words that merely sound alike.

Poetry also comes in fixed and open forms. The sonnet is a fourteen-line poem in iambic pentameter with a set rhyme scheme, existing in an Italian or Petrarchan variety, which turns on an eight-line octave and six-line sestet, and an English or Shakespearean variety of three quatrains and a couplet, whose final two lines often deliver a sharp turn of thought. Other fixed forms include the villanelle, the sestina, and the haiku, each imposing constraints that paradoxically spur invention. Since the nineteenth century, free verse, poetry without regular meter or rhyme, pioneered by Walt Whitman and dominant in modern practice, has sought its music through rhythm, image, and line alone.

Beyond sound and form, poetry works through compression and image. It says much in little, trusting the reader to unfold meanings packed into a few charged words, and it thinks in concrete pictures. Reading poetry rewards patience: reading aloud to hear the music, attending to where lines break and sentences run on, and dwelling on individual words, whose sound, rhythm, and multiple senses all carry the poem's meaning at once.

sections.heading: Narrative: Story, Plot, and Point of View
sections.body:
Narrative, the telling of a story, is the most widespread literary mode, encompassing the epic, the novel, the short story, and much drama and film. To study narrative is to ask how a sequence of events is transformed into a told story, and a first, clarifying distinction separates story from plot. The story is the raw material, the events in their chronological order; the plot is the arrangement of those events in the telling, with its selections, orderings, gaps, and emphases. E. M. Forster illustrated the difference: the king died and then the queen died is a story, a mere sequence, whereas the king died and then the queen died of grief is a plot, because it supplies a causal connection. A narrative may open in the middle of things, withhold information, reorder events, or accelerate and slow time, and these are the storyteller's essential resources.

Plots have long been analyzed for their shape. The classical account, refined by Gustav Freytag for drama, traces a rise through exposition and complication to a climax, followed by a falling action and resolution, driven throughout by conflict, whether between characters, within a character, or between a character and circumstance. Not all narratives follow this arc; many modern works fragment or refuse it, but conflict and change of some kind remain narrative's engine.

The single most consequential choice in telling a story is point of view, the perspective from which it is narrated, because it controls what the reader knows and how they judge it. A first-person narrator, speaking as I, offers intimacy and immediacy but sees only what one character can see and may be unreliable, mistaken, biased, or deceptive, so that the reader must read against the narration to reach the truth, as in the famous case of the narrator of a story who cannot be trusted. A third-person narrator, speaking of he and she, may be omniscient, knowing all characters' thoughts and ranging freely across time and place, or limited, confined to the perspective of a single character while still using the third person. Related is narrative distance, how close the telling stands to a character's mind, from cool external report to the intimate rendering of thought known as free indirect discourse, and the stream of consciousness that follows the flow of a mind.

Alongside these formal elements sit the substance of narrative: character, the invented persons whose desires and choices drive the action and whom E. M. Forster distinguished as flat, built around a single trait, or round, complex and capable of surprising us; and setting, the time and place in which the action unfolds, which supplies not only backdrop but atmosphere, constraint, and meaning. Attending to who tells the story, in what order, with what selection, and at what distance reveals that a narrative's power lies less in what happens than in how the happening is shaped and disclosed.

sections.heading: Drama and the Theatrical Text
sections.body:
Drama is literature written to be performed, and this distinguishing fact governs everything about it. A play is a peculiar kind of text, at once something to be read and a blueprint for a live event; its full existence occurs only in performance, before an audience, through actors, in a shared space and time. To study drama is therefore to read a script while imagining its realization, attending both to the words on the page and to the theatrical life those words are meant to summon.

Because a play, in its purest form, has no narrator to explain, describe, or enter characters' minds, it must convey everything through what characters say and do. This constraint gives rise to drama's characteristic techniques. Dialogue carries the weight that narration bears in fiction, revealing character, advancing action, and supplying information; skilled dramatists make speech do many things at once. The soliloquy, a speech delivered by a character alone on stage, lets the audience hear thoughts that would otherwise be hidden, as in Hamlet's meditations, while the aside briefly shares a character's private reaction. Stage directions, the playwright's instructions for action, setting, and delivery, guide the wordless dimension of meaning.

Western drama descends from ancient Greece, where tragedy and comedy took shape in civic festivals. Aristotle's Poetics, the founding work of dramatic criticism, analyzed tragedy as the imitation of a serious and complete action, arousing pity and fear so as to accomplish a katharsis, a purging or clarification of those emotions. He identified plot as the soul of tragedy and described how the greatest tragic plots turn on a reversal of fortune and a recognition, a moment of fatal understanding, often precipitated by the protagonist's own error or flaw, the hamartia. These concepts still frame discussion of tragedy from Sophocles to the present.

Comedy, tragedy's ancient counterpart, characteristically moves from disorder and obstruction toward harmony and renewal, often ending in reconciliation or marriage, and it works through wit, incongruity, and the exposure of folly. Between and beyond these poles lie many forms: the history play, the tragicomedy, the farce, the melodrama, and the varied experiments of modern theater. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries brought realism, which sought to present life truthfully on stage, and its many reactions, including the symbolic, expressionist, and absurdist theaters, the last, associated with Samuel Beckett, dramatizing a world drained of clear meaning.

For the reader, drama demands an active theatrical imagination. Meaning in a play arises not only from language but from silence, gesture, movement, spectacle, timing, and the physical relationships of bodies in space, none fully specified on the page. Every performance is an interpretation, and no two are identical, which is why the same script yields endlessly different productions. Studying drama thus means reading for performance, asking constantly how words become action and how a written text becomes a living event.

sections.heading: Figurative Language and Literary Devices
sections.body:
Literary writing is saturated with figurative language, expressions that mean something other than, or more than, their literal sense, and learning to recognize and interpret these figures is among the most practical skills of literary study. A figure of speech does not merely ornament a plain statement; it thinks, compressing perception and feeling into forms that literal language cannot achieve, and it often carries the deepest meaning of a passage.

The master figures are the tropes of comparison. A simile compares two things explicitly, using like or as, as in my love is like a red, red rose, inviting the reader to see one thing in terms of another while keeping them distinct. A metaphor asserts the comparison outright, identifying one thing with another, as in all the world's a stage, collapsing the distance and demanding that we transfer qualities from the vehicle, the image, to the tenor, the subject. Metaphor is not a special poetic trick but pervades ordinary thought, as scholars George Lakoff and Mark Johnson showed, so that we habitually speak of argument as war and time as money. Related figures include personification, granting human qualities to nonhuman things, as when the wind sighs; metonymy, naming something by an associated thing, as the crown for the monarchy; and synecdoche, naming a whole by a part, as hands for workers.

A second family of figures works through contrast and indirection. Irony says one thing while meaning another, in its simplest verbal form saying the opposite of what is meant, but extending to situational irony, where events turn out contrary to expectation, and dramatic irony, where the audience knows what a character does not, a device that generates suspense and pathos in tragedy. Hyperbole exaggerates for effect, litotes understates, often through negation, and paradox states an apparent contradiction that conceals a truth, as in the child is father of the man.

Beyond these local figures lie larger structures of meaning. A symbol is a concrete thing that carries a larger significance beyond itself, as a journey may stand for a life or a river for time, and unlike a simple metaphor its meaning is often open and accretive, gathering associations across a work. An allegory extends symbolism systematically, so that a whole narrative operates as a sustained figure, its characters and events representing abstract ideas or a second story. Allusion enriches a text by referring to another work, myth, or event, summoning its resonance in few words. Imagery, the pattern of sensory detail, and motif, a recurring image or idea, build meaning through repetition.

Interpreting figures is not decoding a fixed cipher but a disciplined act of imagination: identifying the two terms a figure yokes together, asking what qualities transfer between them, and noticing why this figure, here, does work no literal phrase could. Attending to figurative language turns reading from the extraction of a message into the experience of how meaning is made.

sections.heading: Reading Closely: The Art of Interpretation
sections.body:
At the heart of literary study lies a practice rather than a body of facts: close reading, the slow, attentive analysis of a text's language to understand how it produces meaning and effect. This method, developed and taught systematically in the twentieth century, treats a poem, passage, or scene as an object worth dwelling on word by word, on the conviction that in literature the smallest choices, a repeated sound, an odd word, a shift of tense, carry significance. To read closely is to resist the impulse to summarize and move on, and instead to ask, of each detail, how it works and why it is there.

Close reading attends to several layers at once. It notices diction, the specific words chosen and their connotations, the associations and feelings a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning, so that home differs from house and slender from skinny though the denotations overlap. It attends to syntax, the arrangement of words into sentences, since a long, delaying sentence and a short, blunt one create different effects, and a sentence's structure can enact its meaning. It listens for sound and rhythm, and it tracks imagery and figurative language, noticing patterns, recurrences, and tensions. Above all it looks for the places where a text is doing something interesting, an ambiguity, a contradiction, a surprising word, a break in pattern, and treats these not as flaws to be smoothed away but as clues to the work's deeper concerns.

An interpretation is a claim about what a text means or how it achieves its effects, supported by evidence drawn from the text itself. This distinguishes literary interpretation from mere opinion or free association: a reading must be argued and grounded in specific features of the language, and it can be more or less persuasive depending on how much of the text it accounts for and how well it fits the details. Good interpretation prizes the evidence of the words on the page over the reader's unchecked impressions, and it welcomes the challenge of contrary evidence.

Interpretation must also navigate a real hazard. To find in a text a meaning it will not bear, to impose a reading against the grain of the words, is over-reading; to miss what is plainly present is under-reading. The discipline offers no formula for the balance, but it insists that claims answer to the text. Ambiguity, the coexistence of multiple valid meanings, is not a problem to be eliminated but often a source of literary richness, and the critic William Empson devoted a famous study to its seven types.

Crucially, literary works rarely have a single correct meaning to be decoded. A great text sustains multiple defensible interpretations and rewards rereading, disclosing new facets over a lifetime. The aim of close reading is therefore not to solve a work but to deepen and discipline one's engagement with it, and to make one's understanding accountable to what the text actually says.

sections.heading: Literary History, Periods, and Movements
sections.body:
Literature is not a timeless collection of masterpieces floating free of history but a stream of works produced in particular times and places, shaped by and responding to their circumstances and to one another. Literary history is the study of this development, of how forms, styles, and concerns arise, dominate, and give way, and it supplies the context without which individual works are only half understood. A satire loses its point when we forget what it attacked; a poem's originality is invisible until we know the conventions it broke.

Scholars organize this stream into periods and movements, useful simplifications that must be handled with care. A period, such as the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, or the Victorian era, groups the literature of a stretch of time marked by shared conditions and tendencies. A movement, such as Romanticism, Realism, or Modernism, names a self-conscious or retrospectively identified program of aesthetic aims shared by a group of writers. These labels are inventions of later critics as much as facts of the past; their boundaries are fuzzy, their members diverse, and no writer fits a label perfectly, but they let us see patterns and describe change.

The broad arc of the Western tradition offers orientation. Classical antiquity produced the epics of Homer and Virgil and the Greek dramatists, and its forms and standards shaped everything after. The medieval period gave allegory, romance, and works such as Dante's Divine Comedy. The Renaissance revived classical learning and produced Shakespeare and the flowering of drama and lyric. The eighteenth century, an age of reason and satire, saw the rise of the novel. Romanticism, from the late eighteenth century, exalted feeling, imagination, nature, and the individual against neoclassical restraint. The nineteenth century brought the great age of Realism in the novel, aiming to depict ordinary life truthfully. Modernism, in the early twentieth century, responding to rapid change and to the trauma of the First World War, broke with traditional forms through fragmentation, interior monologue, and difficulty, in the work of writers such as T. S. Eliot, James Joyce, and Virginia Woolf. Postmodernism later turned to irony, playfulness, and skepticism about grand narratives.

This map is deliberately partial, and its Western focus is itself a limitation the discipline now works to correct. The literatures of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Americas have their own long and rich histories, traditions, and periodizations, and the modern study of world literature and of postcolonial writing has expanded the canon far beyond its old European center. Literary movements also arise in reaction, each generation defining itself against its predecessors, so that history proceeds as a conversation across time. For the student, the value of literary history is not the memorizing of labels and dates but the capacity to place a work in its moment, to hear it answering the works before it, and to recognize both what it shares with its age and how it exceeds it.

sections.heading: Schools of Literary Criticism and Theory
sections.body:
Literary criticism is the reasoned discussion, analysis, and evaluation of literature, and literary theory is the study of the assumptions and methods that underlie such discussion, of what literature is, how meaning arises, and what questions are worth asking. Over the past century the field has generated a succession of theoretical schools, each proposing a distinct lens through which to read, and knowing them equips a reader to see a text from many angles rather than one.

Early twentieth-century criticism sought to make the study of literature rigorous by focusing on the text itself. The Russian Formalists and, later, the Anglo-American New Critics insisted that a work's meaning resides in its words and structure, not in the author's biography or the reader's feelings, and they warned against the intentional fallacy, judging a work by the author's supposed intention, and the affective fallacy, judging it by its emotional effect. Their method of intense close reading remains foundational even for critics who reject their exclusions.

Later theory reopened what formalism had bracketed, connecting literature to language, mind, society, and power. Structuralism, drawing on Saussure's linguistics, sought the underlying systems and codes that make meaning possible, treating individual works as instances of larger structures. Post-structuralism, associated with Jacques Derrida and the practice of deconstruction, radicalized this, arguing that language is unstable, that texts undermine their own apparent meanings, and that no final, fixed interpretation is possible. Psychoanalytic criticism, deriving from Freud, reads texts for unconscious desires, symbols, and conflicts. Marxist criticism reads literature in relation to economic and class conditions, asking whose interests a work serves and how it reflects or contests the social order.

From the 1970s onward, criticism turned decisively to identity, power, and exclusion. Feminist criticism examines how literature represents women and gender, recovers neglected women writers, and analyzes the workings of patriarchy in texts and in the canon itself. Gender and queer theory extend this to the construction of gender and sexuality. Postcolonial criticism, following Edward Said's Orientalism, studies the literature of empire and its aftermath, how the West imagined the peoples it colonized, and the writing that resists and reworks that legacy. New Historicism reads literary and nonliterary texts together as part of a single web of a period's discourses and power relations. Reader-response criticism shifts attention to the reader's active role in making meaning.

No single school holds the field, and most working critics draw eclectically on several. The value of theory for a student is not allegiance to one doctrine but expanded vision: each lens reveals what others miss, a Marxist reading exposing class, a feminist reading gender, a formalist reading craft, so that the same novel yields different, complementary truths. Theory can overreach, imposing a system on a text or dissolving the work into abstraction, and the best criticism keeps returning to the words on the page, using theory to sharpen attention rather than to replace it.

sections.heading: The Canon, Literary Value, and Who Decides
sections.body:
Behind every course, anthology, and library shelf lies a set of choices about which works count as important, and the sum of these choices is the canon, the body of literature a culture treats as central, worth teaching, preserving, and returning to. The canon is not written down as a fixed list, yet it is powerfully real: it shapes what students read, what critics discuss, and what survives. Examining how it is formed, and questioning it, has become one of literary study's most important and contested activities.

The traditional view held that the canon reflects intrinsic and enduring quality, that great works rise to prominence and stay there because of their superior artistry, depth, and universal appeal, tested and confirmed across generations. On this account the canon is a distillation of the best that has been thought and said, in Matthew Arnold's phrase, and its authority rests on collective judgment over time. There is something to this: works that continue to move and reward readers across centuries and cultures do seem to possess uncommon power, and the fact that Shakespeare still fills theaters is not merely an accident of fashion.

Yet from the 1970s onward, this view came under searching critique, in what were called the canon wars. Critics observed that the traditional canon was overwhelmingly composed of works by white European men, and they asked whether this reflected pure merit or the exclusions of the societies that formed it, the historical denial to women and colonized peoples of education, publication, and critical attention. If whole groups were barred from writing and from being read, then the canon records not simply the best writing but the writing that a narrow group was positioned to produce and to value. On this view, judgments of literary value are never innocent of power; they are made by particular people, in particular institutions, with particular assumptions, and they can be revised.

The result has been a broadening rather than a demolition of the canon. Neglected writers, many of them women, writers of color, and writers from formerly colonized nations, have been recovered and admitted, and the category of world literature has widened the field far beyond Europe. Few now argue that all works are equally good or that value is purely arbitrary, but most accept that the canon is a human construction, always provisional, that reflects the interests and blind spots of those who make it and that must be continually re-examined.

This leaves the student with genuinely open questions rather than settled answers. Is literary value objective, subjective, or something formed in the interaction of works and communities of readers over time? Can we judge works across very different cultures and eras by common standards, or must judgment be relative to context? These are not obstacles to literary study but part of its substance, and thinking about them clarifies what we are doing whenever we call one book great and pass over another.

sections.heading: Author, Text, and Reader: Where Meaning Lives
sections.body:
A question runs beneath all the practices of literary study and deserves to be faced directly: where does the meaning of a literary work reside? Three answers have contended, each locating meaning in a different place, in the author, in the text, or in the reader, and the history of modern criticism can be told as a shifting of emphasis among them. Understanding the debate helps a reader see what is at stake in any act of interpretation.

The oldest answer places meaning in the author. On this view, to understand a work is to recover what the writer intended to say, and biography, letters, and historical circumstance are the road to that intention. This approach has obvious appeal and remains the common-sense default, yet it faces real difficulties. Authors' intentions are often unknown, and even when stated they may not match what the work achieves; a text can mean more, or other, than its maker consciously planned. The New Critics named the assumption that meaning equals intention the intentional fallacy and set it aside, and in 1967 Roland Barthes announced the death of the author, arguing provocatively that a text should be freed from the tyranny of its creator and read as a tissue of language open to the reader.

The second answer, dominant in mid-century, places meaning in the text itself. The work is treated as a self-sufficient verbal object whose meaning is contained in its words, structure, and internal relations, available to any competent close reader without recourse to the author's life or the reader's psychology. This approach yielded the disciplined attention to language that remains literary study's core skill, but taken to an extreme it treats the text as sealed off from the world and pretends to an objectivity that the endless disagreement of skilled readers belies.

The third answer places meaning in the reader. Reader-response theory argues that a text is only marks on a page until a reader activates it, and that meaning is produced in the encounter between text and reader, who brings expectations, knowledge, and imagination to fill the text's gaps and realize its potential. Since readers differ, and since the same reader changes over time, meaning becomes plural and dynamic. The danger here is the opposite of the textualist's: if meaning is wholly the reader's creation, then any reading is as good as any other, and the text disappears.

Most thoughtful critics now hold that these are not exclusive rivals but partial truths, and that meaning arises in the interaction among all three: an author's words, shaped by intention and circumstance, structured into a text with its own constraints, and realized by readers who bring the work to life within limits the words impose. The text constrains but does not dictate; the reader creates but is not free to make it mean anything. Holding this middle ground, neither making the author sovereign nor the reader omnipotent nor the text a closed machine, is the mature stance from which interpretation proceeds.

sections.heading: Studying Literature in Practice, and Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
Having surveyed what literature is and how it is analyzed, it remains to describe what studying literature actually involves and to clear away misunderstandings that deter or mislead new readers. Literary study is not the memorizing of plots, authors, and dates, nor the hunt for hidden messages the teacher already knows, nor the passive reception of received opinions about great books. It is a set of skills and habits of mind, exercised on texts, that transfer far beyond the classroom.

The core activity is careful reading followed by argued writing. One reads a text closely, attending to its language and form; one arrives at an interpretation, a defensible claim about how the work means or works; and one supports that interpretation with evidence drawn from the text, quoting and analyzing specific passages rather than merely asserting. The literary essay, the discipline's characteristic product, is an exercise in exactly this: making a debatable claim and proving it from the words on the page, anticipating objections, and reasoning carefully. This trains a rare and valuable capacity, to notice detail, to reason from evidence to conclusion, to entertain ambiguity without collapsing it prematurely, and to communicate a complex understanding clearly.

Several misconceptions are worth dispelling. The first is that a literary work has one correct meaning that the reader must guess. In truth, rich works sustain multiple defensible interpretations, and the goal is not the single right answer but the well-supported reading; some interpretations are nonetheless better than others, judged by how fully and faithfully they account for the text. The second is that analysis destroys enjoyment, that dissecting a poem kills it. Experience suggests the reverse: understanding how a work achieves its effects deepens rather than diminishes the pleasure, as knowing music enriches listening. The third is that symbols and meanings are arbitrary inventions of critics; interpretation is disciplined by evidence, and a reading that the text will not support is simply wrong. The fourth is that literature is a luxury detached from real life; in fact it is one of humanity's chief means of exploring experience, morality, and the minds of others.

That last point names literature's enduring value and its connections onward. By inhabiting other lives and perspectives, literature cultivates imagination and, many argue, empathy, the capacity to grasp how the world looks from inside another person. It preserves and transmits culture, memory, and language across generations. It refines our command of language itself, the medium of nearly all thought and communication. And it connects to every other field: to history, which it illuminates and by which it is illuminated; to philosophy, whose questions about meaning, ethics, and identity it dramatizes; to psychology, linguistics, and the arts. To study literature well is to become a better, more attentive reader not only of books but of the world, and that is why, across every culture and age, human beings have kept telling, preserving, and pondering their stories.
